slides.label: Holonomy
slides.notes: Open by making holonomy a measurement, not a mysterious abstraction. The loop is oriented, the tangent vector is transported all the way around, and only when it returns to the starting tangent plane do we compare the teal and orange arrows. For the notebook's model loop, area is about 4.924, curvature is 0.34, and the returned angle is about 1.674 radians, so the class can see R(L) behaving like curvature accumulated over area.

slides.label: The Measurement Rules
slides.notes: This slide prevents the main misreading. Path arrows show traversal order, while tangent arrows show the transported probe. The vector is not compared pointwise with distant tangent planes; it is carried by the connection and compared only at the basepoint. Along geodesic sides, the transported vector keeps a constant angle with the side, which is why later triangle arguments can become angle bookkeeping.

slides.label: Sphere Octant
slides.notes: Use the unit sphere octant as the first exact computation. The loop follows three great-circle edges, each interior angle is pi over two, and the spherical excess is pi over two. The notebook's transport calculation returns the same angle, so this is the clean positive-curvature case: holonomy equals area equals angular excess.

slides.label: Triangle Ledger
slides.notes: The ledger turns the geometry into a compact identity. If phi_i are the exterior turns of the geodesic sides, then the returned rotation is 2 pi minus their sum. Substituting phi_i equals pi minus theta_i gives theta_1 plus theta_2 plus theta_3 minus pi. The point is that holonomy is angle defect, not the visible bending of the drawn boundary.

slides.label: Hyperbolic Sign
slides.notes: Now the same triangle logic runs in negative curvature. In the upper-half-plane model the drawn angles are conformal, so the Euclidean-looking vertex angles are the hyperbolic angles, but area is hyperbolic area. The sample angle sum is about 2.55071 radians, below pi, giving defect area 0.590882 and returned angle R equals negative 0.590882.

slides.label: Additivity
slides.notes: Additivity is a proof mechanism rather than a new example. When a region is subdivided, every inserted internal edge is traversed once in each direction. Transport forward and then backward along that same edge composes to the identity, so the only uncanceled transport is on the outer boundary. The notebook's sphere check has subareas summing to the whole area with residual near 2.22 times 10 to the minus 16.

slides.label: Infinitesimal Curvature
slides.notes: This slide connects holonomy to Gaussian curvature itself. For large loops on variable-curvature surfaces, R divided by area is an average-like quantity. Shrink the loop around a point and the ratio approaches K at that point. The notebook's constant-curvature samples are intentionally simple: the sphere ratios sit at plus one and the hyperbolic ratios sit at minus one.

slides.label: Spherical Wedge Lab
slides.notes: The parameter lab changes only the longitude width Theta of a spherical wedge. On the unit sphere, both the wedge area and the returned angle equal Theta, so the table is a compact sign and units check. Have students predict the holonomy at 75 or 120 degrees before reading the row, then point out the zero numerical error up to floating point precision.

slides.label: Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by threading the chapter together. Holonomy starts as a returned-angle measurement, exact geodesic triangles turn it into angular excess or defect, subdivision makes the measurement additive, and shrinking loops turns the returned angle per area into Gaussian curvature. The final slogan is that curvature can be detected by carrying a tangent vector around a loop and reading the angle it brings back.
